wine.name: Chevalier-Montrachet
wine.classification: Grand Cru of the Côte de Beaune
wine.sites: Chevalier-Montrachet, the grand cru on the upper slope above Le Montrachet, at about 265 to 290 metres and wholly within Puligny-Montrachet, on thin, stony soil over marl and marly limestone; the vines are farmed biodynamically.
wine.making: Fermented in oak barrels, about a quarter of them new, and aged in them for about twelve months, then moved to stainless steel tank for about six months more on its lees before it is bottled at the domaine.
wine.glass: Acacia and lime blossom, white peach and lemon zest over hazelnut and crushed chalk; taut and slow to open, a fine, stony line rather than richness, with a long, saline finish.
wine.ageing: Closed for its first five to eight years, it opens slowly and keeps for twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle for an hour; a wide white Burgundy glass.

label.means: The grand cru, its own appellation, on the slope above Le Montrachet in Puligny.
The rank above Premier Cru, printed beneath the vineyard's name.
The family domaine of Puligny, distinct from Olivier Leflaive, a négociant house of the village.

records.table: Just above Le Montrachet, on thin and stony soil, Leflaive farms its Chevalier-Montrachet biodynamically and raises it in barrel, then tank. Taut, chalky and slow to open, more line than richness, it is a white that gains from air when young.
records.story: The Leflaive family has been rooted in Puligny since 1717, by the domaine's own account, but the domaine took its present shape in the early twentieth century, when Joseph Leflaive (1870 to 1953), a naval engineer, came home to a village whose vines phylloxera had laid low. He bought vineyards one by one and replanted them on grafted rootstocks, parcel by parcel. After his death in 1953 two of his sons ran the domaine together until the early 1990s. In 1990 the daughter of one of them, Anne-Claude Leflaive (1956 to 2015), came to share the direction with a cousin and began biodynamic trials on a small plot; from 1994 she led the domaine alone, and by 1997 she had put the whole estate under biodynamic farming. In the early 1990s the domaine also added a small parcel of Le Montrachet. Chevalier-Montrachet is the wine it leads with: its parcels sit on the stony upper slope above Le Montrachet, well above Bâtard lower down, and give a narrower, more chiselled wine than Bâtard. Les Pucelles, the premier cru beside Bienvenues, is the one argued for promotion; the Chevalier is the house's grand cru measure. Its virtues are line and patience, and it asks the same of whoever opens it.

wine.name: Meursault Premier Cru Les Perrières
wine.sites: Les Perrières, on the southern side of Meursault towards Puligny, on thin, stony soil over limestone; its name recalls the stone quarries once worked there, many of them since filled and planted.
wine.making: Fermented with its own yeasts in oak barrels, about a third of them new by the domaine's account, with the malolactic coming late, in spring; the wine then rests on its lees for well over a year, close to two by the domaine's sheets, before bottling at the domaine. The vines have been farmed biodynamically since 1998.
wine.glass: Lemon, ripe pear and hazelnut over crushed stone and a flinty, smoky note; broad yet taut, with brown butter in the middle and a long line of firm acidity.
wine.ageing: Generous young, it closes for a few years and then keeps for fifteen to twenty.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle briefly; a wide white Burgundy glass.

records.table: Meursault has no grand cru, and Lafon's Meursault Perrières comes from the stony premier cru towards Puligny most often argued for one. Raised in barrel for well over a year, it is broad yet taut, with hazelnut, ripe pear and a flinty edge, and keeps for twenty years.
records.story: The founder was no Burgundian: born in the Tarn-et-Garonne in 1864, he was an inspector of the public registry, and in 1894 he married into the Boch family, merchants and growers of Meursault. The domaine grew from his wife's inheritance and from later purchases and exchanges, and came to hold Perrières, Genevrières and Charmes, the walled Clos de la Barre around the family house and a parcel of Le Montrachet. In 1918 the Holy See made him a papal count, in thanks for his refusal, as an inspector, to make the clergy declare their wealth, and the domaine's name carries the title. In 1923, as mayor of Meursault, he revived the Paulée, the feast that closes the harvest, inviting thirty five friends to dine in his vat room. After his death most of the vines were let to sharecroppers, and in 1956 his grandson stepped in to stop the domaine being sold. In the mid 1980s the founder's great grandson took charge, ended the last sharecropping leases by 1993, farmed biodynamically from 1998 and in 1999 bought a second estate in the Mâconnais, the Héritiers du Comte Lafon. Les Perrières, stony ground towards Puligny, is the premier cru most often argued for promotion, and here it gains breadth without losing its line.

wine.name: Corton-Charlemagne
wine.classification: Grand Cru of the Côte de Beaune
wine.sites: A small parcel of Corton-Charlemagne, the white grand cru on the high, cool upper slopes of the hill of Corton, which spans Aloxe-Corton, Pernand-Vergelesses and Ladoix-Serrigny.
wine.making: Fermented and aged in oak barrels, a share of them new, for fifteen months to two years by the merchants' accounts, and left long on its lees, which keeps the wine in the reductive, struck match register the domaine is known for; it is bottled at the domaine without filtration.
wine.glass: Struck match and flint over lemon oil, white peach and hazelnut skin; tight and cool, with a firm, chalky line and a long, saline finish.
wine.ageing: Austere for its first five to ten years, it then opens towards hazelnut and honey and keeps for twenty years and more.
wine.serve: 11 to 13 degrees Celsius; decant a young bottle so the struck match note can settle; a wide white Burgundy glass.

records.table: Struck match is the mark of Coche-Dury, a Meursault family domaine, and its Corton-Charlemagne carries it from a small parcel of the white grand cru on the hill of Corton. Tight and saline when young, it opens slowly over many years.
records.story: The hill of Corton carries the name of Charlemagne (about 747 to 814), who held land there and in 775 gave much of the hill to the abbey of Saint-Andoche at Saulieu. A later legend says white grapes were planted on his part of the slope so that red wine would not stain his beard. The hill's white wine kept his name, and on 31 July 1937 a decree made Corton-Charlemagne a white grand cru spread over three communes, with Corton, the red grand cru, sharing the hill. Coche-Dury goes back to a grower who worked vines in Meursault in the 1920s; his son began to sell wine under the family's own label in 1964, and in the 1970s a marriage in the next generation joined the names Coche and Dury. Its wines, from Bourgogne Blanc to the grand cru, rest long on their lees in barrel, with a deliberate reduction that gives a struck match note over citrus and salt, an approach that spread far beyond Burgundy. The domaine passed to the next generation in 2010. The Corton-Charlemagne comes from a small parcel and is made in very small quantity. Keep it, and when its time comes, keep a decanter beside it.

wine.name: Volnay Premier Cru Clos des Ducs
wine.classification: Premier Cru, held whole by the domaine as a monopole
wine.sites: The Clos des Ducs, a premier cru clos beside the village of Volnay, on very calcareous, stony soil over a marly, clay rich subsoil; the vines are farmed biodynamically.
wine.making: Fermented with gentle extraction, pressed gently and run by gravity into oak barrels in the cellars beneath the winery, where it ages for about eighteen months; about a fifth of the barrels are new on average across the domaine's Volnay premiers crus, and the malolactic comes in spring.
wine.glass: Red cherry, raspberry and violet over a cool, stony note; pale, fine and perfumed, with fine, dry tannin and a long, lifted finish.
wine.ageing: Slow to evolve, it reaches its full richness from about ten years, as the domaine tells it, and keeps well beyond that in a strong vintage.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; decant only an old bottle, off its sediment; a wide Burgundy glass.

records.table: Held whole by d'Angerville and named for the Dukes of Burgundy who once owned it, Clos des Ducs is a Volnay premier cru beside the village. Pale, fine and perfumed, Volnay in its silken register, it is served a touch below room temperature.
records.story: From the twelfth to the fifteenth century, by the domaine's account, the Dukes of Burgundy held the vineyard beside Volnay that carries their name. In 1804 a forebear of the family, then sub-prefect of Autun, bought the Clos des Ducs estate, and in 1888 a later heir left it to his nephew and godson, then fifteen, the future Marquis d'Angerville. Phylloxera had ruined the vines, and from 1906 the Marquis, trained at the École des Beaux-Arts rather than in a cellar, replanted them with fine Pinot Noir. In the 1920s he spoke out against the blending of some Beaune merchants; they stopped buying his crop, and he answered by bottling and selling his own wine at the domaine, among the early growers of the Côte d'Or to do so. His stand fed the appellation laws of the 1930s. His son ran the domaine from his father's death in 1952 until his own in 2003, and the next generation turned the vines to biodynamic farming from 2006 and in 2012 founded Domaine du Pélican in the Jura. Clos des Ducs, which the domaine calls its grand vin, is a Volnay premier cru argued for promotion. In the glass it makes Volnay's case: perfume and line rather than weight.

wine.name: Beaune Premier Cru Grèves Vigne de l'Enfant Jésus
wine.classification: Premier Cru: a parcel of the climat Les Grèves held whole by the house
wine.sites: Vigne de l'Enfant Jésus, a parcel in the heart of Les Grèves, the Beaune premier cru on the middle of the slope facing east to south east; the name Grèves recalls its gravelly, almost sandy topsoil over broken limestone, which drains well.
wine.making: Picked by hand into small crates and sorted by hand, among the house's first plots each year. After a few days of cold soak it ferments with punching down, stays on its skins for eighteen to twenty days and goes to a vertical press, then ages for a year or more in French oak barrels, a share of them new.
wine.glass: Red cherry, raspberry and wild strawberry over clove, cinnamon and a soft, earthy note; supple and round, with fine tannin and a gentle, perfumed finish.
wine.ageing: Open and supple young, it ages well for seven to ten years and more by the house's own sheet, and a strong vintage can last for decades.
wine.serve: 15 to 17 degrees Celsius; no need to decant a young bottle; a wide Burgundy glass.

records.table: Once the vineyard of Beaune's Carmelite nuns, Vigne de l'Enfant Jésus is a parcel in the heart of Beaune Grèves that Bouchard has held whole since 1791. Supple and round, with red cherry and a touch of clove, it is a Beaune premier cru that pours well young.
records.story: Michel Bouchard (1692 to 1755), a cloth merchant from the Dauphiné, crossed Burgundy on his way to Flanders and, by the house's account, settled in Beaune in 1731; his son became his partner in 1746, and in 1775 the house bought its first vines, in Volnay Les Caillerets. Vigne de l'Enfant Jésus belonged then to the Carmelite nuns of Beaune. One of them, Sister Marguerite du Saint-Sacrement (1619 to 1648), was devoted to the Infant Jesus and, the story goes, foretold that the long childless queen, Anne of Austria (1601 to 1666), would bear a son; when the future Louis XIV was born in 1638, the vineyard took its name from her devotion. The Revolution took it from the convent, and in 1791 the house bought it at the sale of national property. In 1820 the family bought the Château de Beaune, the fifteenth century royal fortress of Louis XI (1423 to 1483), and its bastions became the house's cellars. In 1995 the Henriot family of Champagne took the helm of the house, and three years later took over Domaine William Fèvre in Chablis. The story of the nun and the King is the one to tell as it is poured.

report: Rechecked with search on 12 November 2026 (eight searches and one refused fetch): the founder's dates, 1731, the partnership of 1746, the first vines of 1775, the purchase of 1791, the Château de Beaune of Louis XI bought in 1820, Clos de la Mousse whole since 1872 and the making of the parcel are the house's own pages, read through search.

Sister Marguerite du Saint-Sacrement's dates rest on two reference accounts; her prophecy is the house's anecdote and is told as a story; the years of Anne of Austria, Louis XIV and Louis XI are those of every history.
The time in barrel is a year or more, since a merchant gives twelve to fourteen months and the house's other premiers crus twelve to twenty; the house's sheet with the figures could not be fetched.
The house's sheet gives 17 to 18 degrees Celsius; the record keeps the Codex's 15 to 17 for a medium red.
The library calls Ancienne Cuvée Carnot a monopole; the house calls it its first purchase in Caillerets, a climat shared with others, so the record says a cuvée.
